blocks.x: I'll start out by saying this is an interview with Mr. Steve Angram and the date is August the 8th, 1961. We're out at his home at 2105 Allen Street. Do you want to give your full name Mr. Angram? Stephen Angram. Any middle name? No, no middle name.

You were saying when you left Chalini, I guess you knew the horn pretty good, but you still not what you'd call a great clarinet player yet. No, no. You still had quite a long ways to go? I had a long ways to go after I left there. Well, how do you figure that you became so good? Well, by playing with different good bands. In other words, picking up ideas? Picking up ideas from other bands. And working them out yourself? Yeah, working them out myself. When I was sitting in a band playing as a good band, I'd get all them ideas and then I'd come home and I'd study them things and I'd practice that, you know? That's what I used to do. In other words, you say that no teacher can make you great. It's more or less got to come out. It's got to come to you. That the feeling's in you. You see, you've got to have that feeling. Once you get the sound and the feeling, then you can come to be great. But if you don't have, some folks can read anything you put in front of you, but they don't have that feeling. Then you don't sound like nothing. You've got to have that feeling. You must have that feeling. You must have the feeling. If you ain't got the feeling, you can't do nothing. But then it seems like there's a lot of work to that too, Steve. A lot of practice to that? You've still got the practice. You've still got the practice. But you'd say playing with a lot of different bands helps too? That helps. In other words, not just one band. Not just one band. Yeah. It's one band. Different band that helps you. Because you're going to play in one band. It's better than this band. Another band is better than that one is better. Then sometimes you might fall back and get in one. It's not so good. You see? Well then, you said the day, you done been in them good bands. You can help that band. It's not so good. You see? You can push him along. Make him sound good. You see? I'm on the table some of the best ones, yeah. When you speak about pushing them along, what does that mean exactly, Steve? That means if a fella, when you're sitting down and you're playing in the band, this fella, you might play a song and he say, well, I don't know that song. Or I can't play in that key. Or you tell him, you say, well, it's lower than sitting in the teacher key. It's lower than G or B or C or whatever key it is. Or A flat, B flat. Maybe he can't play in that key. Well, you tell him, all right. You can't play in that key. But if this number is supposed to be played in that key, then I have to play it in that key. Well, you tell him, you'll hold your horn and say, fill in when you can. You see? You tell him, hold his horn and fill in this one. That's why you feel that you can come in there, then you'll come in. Then he'll come to, you know, he'll come to learn that, you see. And he'll come to be great too and get in all keys, you see. In other words, what you're saying is like to push him is to encourage him? Encourage him, yeah. That's encourage him, you know. Don't love with this Gustafella, you know, when he's doing something, you know. Don't love with this. Just encourage him, you know. Always encourage him, you know. Always give him encouragement, you know, to go ahead on and follow him. You see? Never tell a fella, man, you can't play this, you can't play that. No, don't ever tell him that. Always tell him that he sounds good, you know. That gives him courage.
Sure, he'll do better, man.

Yeah, you'll do better. He'll do better. You're going to try to do better. But if you tell him he don't sound good, you done disgust the man. Yeah, he ain't going to do nothing then. And he will sound bad. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Always tell him he's doing fine. And a man that sort of is needing a little pushing like that, you would play perhaps even more yourself to help him. That's right. To help him alone. Mm-hmm. In other words, you're all working together in the band. Working together in the band, but if he's weak, I'm going to push myself a little harder, you know, to help him, you see? Yeah, so he don't fall, you see? Or like the public out there, they don't know. They don't know what's happening back there, you see? But you're covering him up, you see? But still know, he ain't going to come home. When he leaves that job, he's going home and practice. Don't care what I say, he ain't going to forget it, he's going to practice. Think about them things, you know? When you get on another, when you hear him again, he'll hear him by himself, he'll be ready to sing. Yeah. What other bands did you play with Steve? Well, I played with all, my Clayton's band, I played with him along with any band in the city. Who? Kid Clayton. Played with him along with anybody. I played with Rene, but not stationary, you know? Used to play a penny job with Kid Rene. And I played with Punch, a little while not stationary. I played with Chris Kelly, a long time too.
What is that for water now? Who was your favorite trumpet player in those days that you liked to work with?
I used to like to work with Chris.
Yeah.

Chris Kelly did? He played plenty of music. And the hard music. And he put that music up there and tell you, you're going to play this music. Chris Kelly did? Yeah, he's dead now. Yeah. But he did that, didn't he? Yeah, he did. That's what he used to do. No, you're going to play this. Put it up there. You had to have a music stand. Play in this band. Every band in this band had a music stand. Come on his job, you had a music stand. About what year was this Steve? Huh? About what year was this, how old would you be then? Then I was around 32 or 33 years old then. In other words that would be in the late 20s or early 30s? Early 30s. Early 30s. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. What kind of music did he have on this time? Was it popular music? Yeah. Yeah. He first had all of his music. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. For me. Chris had all popper music.
The record stock orchestration that they drive? That's right. New York?
Yeah. He used to get his music from New York. Now I just saw this piece here about Gailers Boyd, I guess you heard of that. Gailers March? Yeah. Gailers March, you know. Yeah. He had that.
Had the music for that.
Had the music for that.
He never seen the music for that.

Yeah. He had the music. Yeah, you know, but Chris had the music for it. Mm-hmm. Who else was in his band when you played with him? He had Red Happy, you know, he's dead too. Drummer. Drummer, yeah. I guess you heard of him. I never got to know him. Yeah. Big fella you call Ike. Big Ike Robinson. Ike Robinson is still on Bell Cravo on stage. He was playing with him.
We talked to him a couple months ago.
Yeah, he was playing with him.
That's right, he told us about, what was it, the sixes or something? He used to play a lot. Yeah. Three sixes. Yeah.
That was the blues, I guess.
Yeah. The blues, he could play blues too. Did that guitar player or bass or something? Yeah, he had a guitar player.

Used to use this boy, let's see what his name is. Used to live on San Francisco's feet. He's dead too. He used to use Walter Preston a good bit too in his band. You know Walter? I didn't know him. I've heard of him. Well, Walter was playing with him the time he died and I was playing with him when he died. He was playing with him in his band. What kind of jobs did you get mostly with Chris Kelly? You were in the dance hall? Dance hall. Yeah, people used to give plenty dances. You know? Big dance hall. See that Italian hall out there on Esplanade Street? Oh yeah. We done played a many dances in that hall. Many big dances we done played in there. We had done everything. That used to be our regular place we used to play at all the time. Like carnival, carnival day, carnival night, all the mighty law dances, you know? Carnival dances, you know like in carnival coming in. We used to play all of them dances. Chris had a real good band.
Just always a small band, was it about six or seven or how many? He used seven pieces in his band. Yeah.

About what day? He used cramettes, cram bones, and then he used the alto sax. Who played alto? Followed by Robert Horne, he was a cramettes player. He played alto sax with me. Sometime when I used to be working, Robert Horne used to dub them. He played the clarinet and his sax. Did you ever touch the clarinet, Steve? You mean the sax? You mean the sax? No, I never didn't bother with it. No. I just loved that clarinet. I didn't like no sax. I loved that clarinet.
Did you ever play an E-flat clarinet or have an A clarinet? No, no, I never played either one of those.
Or played the A-flat.
Or played the B-flat. Or played the B-flat. Or played the B-flat. Did you ever try a B-flat system?

No, I never cried that either. I don't know if I can clear them, but I'm more out of the night than I can though. You can learn it, sure. Yeah. I think the alibi sounds better, don't you, Steve? To me, it's got a heavier tone. I think so. That's what I've got. You've got an alibi. Yeah, to me, it's got a heavier tone. I know this, I know this, whenever you're on parades, I can hear you crying down the street before I hear the trumpet. Yeah. Yeah, yeah. I can really hear you. Yeah. Mm-hmm. I think probably you're about the strongest street fire around now. Yeah. That's true. That's really, I know that. That's the real fact. Yeah. The rest of them folks can't reach it like that. No, they sure can.

In the old days, did most of the fellas on the street use an E flat or the big one? E flat. That's right, the little one, E flat, most of them. None of them couldn't pay no B home. I'm forgetting now who started that dog.
I think Willie Hunter was the one. He used to go E flat too. On a parade. He quit. He wanted to use the B flat. Yeah.
Mm-hmm.

I went off and he used B flat climbing on the parade, but still no, he don't get up there and make the modern note. No. No. Do you think that playing the sax might spoil them a little bit for a crying act? It do. Do you think that? It does, yeah. Mm-hmm. I've sort of noticed that myself. Yeah, I do. It seems like you get a different armature for that big- For that big mouthpiece. Yeah. Yeah. It's for the cranny. Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Well, I was going to ask about the Tushaline when he taught, did he have you bite onto the upper part of the mouthpiece of your teeth on?

Did you ever cover your both lips? Yeah, he always taught you to put the horn in the direct center. You see? Of your mouth. Of your mouth. Yeah, and don't let it touch your bottom teeth. What is it? Don't touch your bottom teeth, but you can touch, you know, the top. Yeah, bite onto the upper teeth. On the upper teeth, yeah. But you don't, do you actually bite on it, or? No, you don't bite on it. You just, you don't have a hole in it, you know? Yeah, it's a hole. You see, like, press fine, like when you're walking in the street, well, quite naturally, you got to hold it, you know? Yeah. But your bottom teeth don't touch it.
Well, did you know any baronet players that covered, uh, the lips over both teeth, up and down though?
No, I don't know of any.
No. Okay. Daniel Moneta says he, he learned that way from, uh, Sam Dutre, the old man Sam Dutre. Yeah. I know Barney Bigard does that way.
He does, eh? Yeah.

They call it double on the jury. Supposed to be a French system. I just wonder if anybody around here much use that. No, I, I never use that. Yeah. Well, did you ever see that Teo play? Any of the Teo, like, Lorenzo?

Yeah, I seen Lorenzo Teo, sir. How did he do you remember? I don't remember now, this is how he used to do. Oh. I don't remember how to say, but he was a wonderful prayer in that prayer too. He was one of them good ones. Yeah. Well, I noticed your, uh, your mouthpiece is not marked up, uh, at all by your, by your, by your teeth. Yeah. It's not, you, you, you can't have a very heavy pressure on it. No, I don't have no heavy pressure on it. No. No. Because there's no teeth marks on it. No. No. No, I have a teeth marks on it. In other words, you're just holding it. Holding it today. You're not pressing on it. No, I don't press on it. I think most of your pressure must come from your top lip.
Yeah.

Otherwise you need to mark it. See, when you put the hole in your mouth, you see, it's dripping, you hold it down, then you hold it too low, tight like that. See, you know. See. But let the more pressure go on your bottom lip, you see. That's where you come at it. See, if it be touching up here too much, it's going to interfere with your sound, your tone finger. Yeah. You must have quite a bit of pressure on your top lip on that too. Well, not me. I don't have too much pressure on my top lip. No? No. No, I don't have no pressure on my top lip. Rarely. I have pressure, but not much. Not much.
Yeah.
Mm-hmm.
You were wondering about the clarinet. Did you ever try any with the more keys or less keys, like the king keys? Yeah, I tried one.

I had one with 13 keys. Yeah. I used one with 13 keys. Yeah. Yeah. I used one with 13 keys. With the key up top, they look like a button, you know this. That E-flat key looked like a button, yeah. Well, I used one like that. That was with 13 keys. Yeah. That's all it had on. I used that for quite a while. Did you like that?
No, I never really liked it.

Yeah. Because, you know, I would miss them keys, you know, when you get the finger, you know, and making a little reddish, you see, and running over the horn, up and down, you see. You miss them keys, you see. You carry your hand up, you see, like, those keys on the side, you got to hit them, you see. Hit them, you see. Hit them, you see. Coming down, you see. When you got all those 25 keys on there, well, it's quite nice, you know. You see, when you hit them, it's all sound, you know.
What make is your horn now?
Out.
I mean, that's like a...

Oh, hands a metal. Oh, hands a metal, yeah. How long have you had this... I haven't had that horn 20 years. 20 years? Mm-hmm. Where'd you get it from? Oil line. Oil. How many horns have you had altogether? I haven't had about five. Yeah, you have. There he is. Yeah. Yeah, about five horns already. This one, I know, you've got it very, very worn where your fingers go on the whole wood. Yeah, yeah. And it makes you know it's been in service a long time. That's right. You've been putting your fingers on there plenty times. That's right. It's worn down. Yeah, really. And I hate to get rid of that horn. It's a nice horn. Yeah, I hate to get rid of it. I doubt if you'd get another one as good as that now. No. You ain't gonna find nothing as good as that. I don't know. Pound them up. Yeah. And you can't find them the way, the only way you would be able to find them, because them horn would be in the pawn shop. Yeah, brother. The old ones. The old ones, yeah. They don't seem to make them new anymore. No, they don't make the album system new anymore. All the old ones are making our BIM system. Yeah. And those BIM system, they're not all wood either. No. No, they're not all wood. They're something. Hard rubber. Hard rubber. Metal. Yeah. I see you take them out, take them horns in the streets, you know, playing a parade, and the sun is hot. That horn, you can take your finger, you know, and do like that. Yeah, it's soft. Is this just soft? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. My horn there, it don't. No. No. Don't care how hot the sun shines, that horn don't get soft. No. No, it's hard wood, I guess. Hard wood, you see, yeah. Hard wood. I don't know what kind of wood it is, but it's good wood. That's why I don't want to get rid of it. You can't find a real good wooden crown there. Very hard. Yeah, yeah. Oh, I imagine that's good for a long time, that horn of yours. Yeah. Sounds good, no. Yeah. It sounds fine. Let's see now, you made the first record you ever made the other day, didn't you? That's right. First one I ever made. I never made it number four. I never made it anymore. I never made it anymore. Nice. But a note on that, you made it at the corner of Royal and Ursula Line, wasn't it? Yeah, Royal and Ursula Line. Two days ago. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Two days ago. You played with the Sheik? Punch Miller. Punch Miller. Yeah. How did you like that section? I liked that section very well. It was a good section. You didn't get nervous? Well, I was nervous on the first. When I was starting off, I wasn't nervous. I was real nervous. I was wondering how I was going to sound. Yeah. Yeah. You know what I was like making them in front. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You were like getting mad as it seems, isn't it? Sure was. But I was afraid though for a while. I was real nervous. Yeah. Well, that's quite natural. First time you tried. Yeah. I reckon. I was like, I reckon. Yeah.
I reckon.

Mm-hmm. Let's see, we were talking about the Chris Kelly band. Did you play with any other bands like that? Did you ever play with Buddy Petit? No, I never did play with Buddy Petit. How about Rene? Yeah. I played with Rene. When Rene? Well, I played with Rene and not regular. I mean, Rene used to play for Michelin Blunches on a Monday advertising for the, you know, for the store. Every Monday I used to play with Rene. Well, let's say he used to play a lot of high notes on his trumpet. He did. Well, how was that for the coronet to play along with him? It didn't worry me at that time. At that time, I could make high notes too then. It didn't worry me then. See, when he would come down or take down or anything, then I'd, you know, you know like you do when the trumpet take down, then you'd yell for me then. Yeah. When he would take down. Well, when he was playing high, what were you doing? Just playing low? Just playing down in the stage. I would try to buck against him, you know. Just play down in the stage. Variate behind him, make melody behind him, an off chord, you see. But when he'd take down, I'd pick up the lead from him, you see, and then you'd hear me making high notes too, you see. Read the trombone, bass and everything. See? Drum. That'd sound good. When you say variate behind him, you were sort of playing a second part, a harmony part? Yeah, a harmony part. Yeah. Yeah, I noticed you still do a lot of that. Yeah. The other night you were telling me you used to play with Clayton, years ago. Yeah, I did. But didn't you say he played a different style? He didn't blow as loud as he's doing now. Didn't blow as loud? No, Clayton played a lot of cabaret stuff, soft music. He used to use his music. He used to use his music plenty. Then when he would play, he didn't blast his horn. But now it looks like he was up late, he blasts it, you know? He seems to play a lot of high stuff. Yeah, high stuff. Did he play as high in the old days as he does now? No, he didn't play as high as he do now. He was a strong corner, but he didn't reach up, you know, reaching up notes like he do now. I told him the other night, I said, Clayton, I said, you don't lift this sharp tonight? I said, gee, you blowing some high notes? He said, yeah, man. He said, my lips stays like that. I said, you blowing some high, boy. That's why I told him. But do you find it more difficult to play with him now than it was in the ball? No, it's the same thing. Same thing? Same thing, yeah. You just play the same sort of part? That's right. Mm-hmm. Same thing. Do you find the bands nowadays, like the bands over there, St. Peter Street, do you find them about the same as they were in the 20s and 30s? Yeah, they're about the same thing. That's the same thing down in the 30s there. The band over there on St. Peter's, that's the same thing. Same kind of thing. They had nothing different. Mm-hmm. Same thing.

I was going to ask about some of the old times there, Nettis, when you first moved to the city. Did you hear people like Big Eye and Piku and... Yeah. Or was McCurdy around? Do you remember him? I heard of him, but I never heard of him play. I heard of McCurdy. I never heard of him play yet. Did you ever hear George Barquet? Was he hearing when you were in the bar?

Yeah, I haven't heard of Barquet. Barquet used to play with Freddie Kepler. Used to play with Freddie Kepler lots of time. I used to go to dancing. George Barquet was playing. I had to sit right up under the music stand, listen to that man play, crying there. Was he good? He was real good. Right. And he played a whole lot of low register. Low register? Plenty of low register. He'd go up and make them notes, you know, go way up and come down, you know, breathe and just scream, you know, and the way up. Make them pretty, you know. And I'd just sit down under that music stand and listen at it. I'd never go to dance. I'd just sit down and listen at them people play. That's all I used to do is sit and listen at them, you know. No, they'd tell my dancing too much. I used to go to dance near them. Especially if I'd go to a place and a client that was there, man, I'd never was going to dance. You said George Barquet was playing with Freddie Kepler? Yeah. What kind of trumpet player was Freddie Kepler? He was one of them good ones. Was he a good one? Yeah, he was a good one. Freddie Kepler was a trumpet player on all the punch, punch metal. Played something like on punches style. They say he was very powerful. He was powerful. Powerful man. He was big enough. He was a big man? He was a big fella, yeah. About six foot two. Yeah. Weighed about two something. Weighed about two hundred and something.
Who was your favorite clarinetist of all of the old time men that you heard when you were a boy? Who did you like best? I liked Johnny Dawson's best. You got to hear Johnny Dawson?

Yeah. That was my favorite one. He was. Johnny Dawson. I knew him in Chicago. He was wonderful then, I thought. Mm-hmm. Used to play here, man. I'd run. Got to hear that bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo I'd love to hear that man play playing. I noticed you sound, sometimes, some of the things you do sound quite a bit like that. Yeah, I used to listen to him so much. I used to listen to the dots all the time. I'd love to hear that man play. What was it, can there anything special you can say about his playing, particularly your life? Now here's a number I used to love to hear him play. I used to love to hear him play High Society. I used to love to hear Johnny Dutch play High Society. He played High Society different from any other client that I've heard. Different from PQ and all them clients that played. He played High Society different. He never just started from his low notes down here. He started from the top with High Society. He thought when he hit that note, he said, Then he fall down. Then he come right back up again, you see. High Society, you see. And he played that, and that's what I used to like. Who was playing with him in his band? That was his band, was it? Johnny Dutch Band of the Roof Garden? Yeah, Joe Oliver. King Oliver. Oh, was Oliver's band? Yeah. King Oliver was playing. Who else was with him besides Oliver and Doug's? Well, I didn't know them fellas. See, I was young then. Johnny Dutch was the one I used to keep up with, because he was playing the clarinet. He was your favorite. Yeah, he was a lot of favorite, yeah. And those buck-eyed, him and buck-eyed. Of course, I never really care much about the connex, but I was crazy about that clarinet.
Yeah. Did you ever hear Big Eye Louie much? Louie Nelson? Yeah, I never heard him much. I never didn't worry about him too much.
Wasn't one of your favorites, then? No, he wasn't. He was a good clarinet player, though. Man, that's one of them. Freddie Kepler men's, too. He was Freddie Kepler for quite a while, though.

But I never didn't take to him much. What about Piku? How did he rank? Of course, we heard him when he was pretty old, you know. We never heard him when he was really young. Did he sound much different when he was young?

Yeah, he was rough. He was a terrible clarinet player, huh? When he was young, yeah. Oh, you could hear one time was Alphonse Piku. He played with Manuel Perez. He's dead now. In his dance band or street band? He used to play street band and dance band. No, no. Piku was rough. Well, Piku was the target of town. That's right. I mean, Piku was our best musician, you know, out of all them fans up there. He was a good musician. He was a musician. He was a musician. He was a musician. He was a better musician than all them fellas. Peter Borkheimer and Lorenzo Teo, they tell me, he was a good musician, too.
I've heard that he was. His father and uncle were too. He was an old Lorenzo and Papazio. I never did hear any of him.

I never did hear too much of him either, but I used to see him around that time. Yeah. Good kind of thing. Did you ever come across where Hader played the old Sam Lutre, Sam Lutre Sr.? Yeah, I don't know. I played with him. I played with him a couple times, you know. Yeah. Two clarinetes and a band? No, no. He played a ton of sax. Oh, yeah. And clarinet. Is that the old man or the young man that's living now? No, the young one. The young one was living now.

Well, yeah, but his father is supposed to be a clarinetist, too. Yeah. And his uncle, Norey Dutre, was a trombonist of Oliver. They were back in that period. Yeah. Well, I don't know where Norey is. I don't know where they're going to play. I was wondering about a couple of the other clarinetes that I missed, what they were like, for instance. Zeb. Zeb, yeah. You remember Zeb? Zeb, yeah. You ever hear him? Yeah.

What's his name? What's his second name? Do you know? Well, that's all I know is Zeb, Zeb, Zeb, yeah. And another good kind of clarinetes, too. Pills. Now, that's a relation to Zeb. Pills? Pills, yeah. That's a cripple fellow. He had one leg short enough.
What style did they play? What kind? I mean, was it anything like dogs or more like big eye or more like...

Yeah, he played on all those men's pico. Pills, yeah. Pills. Yeah. And them fellows played, what you call those clarinetes? A-cranet. Well, they had different keys. Yeah. The guy going to the job, he had three or four clarinetes, man. They couldn't play in them different, just switching them different keys, you know. Oh. You ever hear Georgie Boyd playing? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Lots of good jazz clarinetes playing. What? Georgie Boyd, yeah. Oh, Georgie Boyd was wonderful. Get up there, Teddy. It's adorable. Yeah, he wanted to get in. Did Georgie Boyd remind you of anybody? I mean, anybody that we've heard? Did he sound like dogs or more like pico or...? Yeah, he sounded like dots. Kind of like dots. Yeah, he sounded like dots, man. That was Punches playing that play. Yeah, I understood he played with Punches playing that play. Yeah, that's Punches playing that play. Yeah, I was trying to do it, too.
Did George Boyd, did he read music much or just mostly...? No, he didn't read much.
He didn't read much.
He could spell a little, but he didn't too much read. Yeah. I think George Lewis says that he liked him, too, and used to maybe copy him some, I don't know.

Yeah, George Lewis used to follow him around. What about your brass band work, Tim? What was the first brass band you played with? The first brass band? George, that's George Wynn band. That's the first brass band I was playing. Oh, yeah? Yeah, that's the first brass band I was playing with. I never played in Northern. How long have you been with your band? I've been playing with George now about ten years. You didn't do any brass band work before that? No. No, I didn't do any brass band work. But you must have heard plenty of that. Yeah, no, no. One of the brass band work I used to do now was when Chris Kelly would hire different men, you know, like when he'd get parades and funerals and things like that. He used to hire different men. Well, you wouldn't call that an organized brass band. That's just a make-up band, you see? That's what Chris used to do. But in other words, you had done street work before. Yeah, I'd done street work before, yeah. But George Williams played regular brass band when I played in. And how do you like it? How do you like the brass band work? I like it. You like it? Yeah. I really like it. Yeah, you look like you're having a lot of fun playing. Yeah, yeah, I like it. Yeah, I like it. It seems like a lot of hard work you don't take down very much when you're playing. No, I don't take down because, I'll tell you for this reason why. Them there, you see those two sacks there? They don't hold no lead. You see? Neither one of them sacks, they have the alto and neither they tenor. So you get them a lead? Yeah, so George, if I do happen to take down, George, he'll hardly, come on Steve, what you gonna do, man? The people don't know where they at. They don't know where they at. Talking about the trumpets, you see, when they take down. See, they got to have a lead for when they come up again, you see?
